pariah

/puh-RYE-uh/ - the stress falls on RYE · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Pariah means an outcast; a person shunned by those around them.

In the novel's third act, the debt collector realizes he has become the island's pariah: shutters latch as he walks the lane, and even the ferryman will not meet his eye.

Example

The critic who panned the town's beloved festival returned the next year a pariah — hoteliers 'lost' his booking, and the shuttle to the fairground was somehow always full.

Pariah is stronger than outsider or misfit because it names someone actively shunned by nearly everyone around them — not merely unknown or awkward, but avoided on purpose, door by door.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

exile: An exile has been forced out of a place and must physically stay away — the distance is geographic. A pariah can stay exactly where they are and still be utterly alone, because it is the people, not the place, that have shut them out.

misfit: A misfit simply does not fit in — awkward, out of step, in the wrong crowd — but nobody is organizing against them. A pariah is made, not born: the group shuns them deliberately, door by door, and keeps on doing it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

insider: someone accepted at the group's center

favorite: the one the group prizes most

Where it sits · how widely they are shut out

outsider → outcast → pariah

outsider vs. pariah: An outsider is a far milder case than a pariah: an outsider simply is not part of the group yet — the door is closed but nobody guards it — while a pariah is actively driven off at every turn.

outcast vs. pariah: Outcast is milder than pariah: an outcast has been pushed out of one circle, while a pariah is shunned by practically everyone, everywhere they turn.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — pariah: from Tamil paraiyar, 'drummer' — a hereditary caste name

Put it together: Pariah cannot be taken apart — it is a whole-word borrowing. It comes from Tamil paraiyar, the hereditary drummers whose caste was ranked among the lowest in southern India; colonial English seized the caste name and widened it to mean anyone utterly shunned. The word's history is itself a record of exclusion, which is worth pausing on when you use it.

Why there's no relative to spot: Because pariah arrived whole from Tamil — one of the few everyday English words that did — it shares no root with anything else you will read. There is no 'pari-' family to spot; the word stands alone, and its drumbeat origin survives only in dictionaries.

Strength Check

Word Choice

strong / journalistic

Pariah is a strong, headline-ready word: states, executives, and neighbors can all be pariahs, but only when the shunning is near-total. For milder cases reach for outcast or outsider. Ostracism, taught in this unit, names the treatment; the pariah is the person it lands on. The word began as a caste name, so it always carries a shadow of unearned exclusion.
